sections.html: The "Grey Ocellatum" belongs to the smaller bushfish species that do not care for their spawn. The largest specimen seen so far was less than 10 cm long. The water temperature should be 24-28°C.

• Needs a tight-fitting lid as this species is known to jump. The tank cover should contain no gaps, as it's a notorious jumper.

The tailspot ctenopoma, Ctenopoma kingsleyae, is an anabantoid with an enormous range, recorded from Mauritania and Senegal to Gabon and the DR Congo. One of the more aggressive members of the genus, it can be particularly nasty towards conspecifics and will eat small fish. It is named after the explorer Mary Kingsley, and there are reports of specimens surviving in aquaria for over 30 years.

Has an enormous natural range throughout much of western and central Africa. It's been recorded in Mauritania, Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ivory Coast, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon and Democratic Republic of Congo.

The species was described in 1938 using a single specimen from the Congo under the name Anabas breviventralis. C. kingsleyae has never been imported alive from the Congo, and all animals sent from there as C. kingsleyae have always been "Grey Ocellatum". The "Grey Ocellatum" occurs together with the "real" Ctenopoma ocellatum.

A single specimen could be housed in a standard 120cm x 30cm x 30cm, 108 litre tank. If you want to keep it with other species, though, a tank of at least 150cm x 45cm x 45cm, about 304 litres, would be needed.

Like other Ctenopoma, this species does best in a dimly lit environment. Either use subdued lighting, or add a layer of floating plants to provide the preferred conditions. Add hiding places in the form of dense thickets of plants, chunks of bogwood, or rocky formations. It's an active species, so leave some areas of the tank open for swimming. The tank cover should contain no gaps, as it's a notorious jumper.
The chemical water composition is irrelevant for the care. The water temperature should be 24-28°C.

It's a predator by nature, and although it does require a meaty diet, there's no need to feed live fish in the aquarium. Prawns, mussels, earthworms and similar foods are all accepted without fuss. Dried foods are taken willingly too.
C. breviventrale is peaceful towards conspecifics and fish that do not serve as food. Plants are not bothered.

This species is a predator and will eat any fish small enough to swallow, so it's definitely not a species for the general community. It's peaceful towards tankmates too large to eat, and towards its own kind given enough space. In a big tank with plenty of cover, it could be combined with other similarly-sized, robust species. A couple of these along with Mormyrids, Synodontis catfish and perhaps some Polypterus would make for an interesting setup. If geography is not an issue, it can be kept with similarly-sized, peaceful cichlids, larger characins, cyprinids and Loricariids.
The fish matures at a length of about 5-6 cm, as can easily be seen from the spiny field behind the eye, which the males develop when they reach sexual maturity.
The male is noticeably spinier around the gill covers and under the eyes.

Rarely achieved in the hobby. Few reports are available. The breeding tank should be large and contain lots of floating plants. The fish usually spawn at night in the typical anabantoid embrace, following a pursuit of the female by her partner. The eggs float to the surface and come to rest in the surface vegetation. It is best to remove the parents at this stage. The fry can be fed infusoria or liquid fry food initially, followed by newly hatched brine shrimp after a few days more. It is thought that C. kingsleyae and other egg-scattering Ctenopoma may well be seasonal spawners as a pair will often spawn regularly for several months and then stop for a while. This does not appear to be related to water temperature or other parameters. There is also a general school of thought that the species doesn't become sexually mature until it reaches 5-10 years old.

This species can be exceptionally long-lived and there are reports of specimens surviving in aquaria for over 30 years. It is named after the explorer Mary Kingsley, and often goes by the common name of Kingsley's climbing perch. While Ctenopoma are closely related to the Asian climbing perch (Anabas sp.), they are not known to have the ability to cross areas of land like this species. Like others in the suborder Anabantoidei, the species possesses an accessory breathing organ known as the labyrinth organ. So-called due to its maze-like structure, this organ allows the fish to breathe atmospheric air to a certain extent. It is formed by a modification of the first gill arch, and consists of many highly vascularised, folded flaps of skin. The structure of the organ varies in complexity between species, tending to be more well-developed in those inhabiting particularly oxygen-deprived conditions.

The "Grey Ocellatum", as labyrinth fish lovers call this species, is a good example of knowledge gained through aquaristics. With regard to body proportions, fin ray numbers, scale formula, etc., many bushfish species cannot be reliably distinguished from each other, so old, discoloured specimens preserved in alcohol are of little use in this regard. Ctenopoma breviventrale is today considered synonymous with C. kingsleyae, the Tailspot bushfish (cá bụi đốm đuôi), by many scientists who have never seen the living animals. The species name breviventralis is an adjective and must agree in gender with the genus name: Anabas is masculine, hence breviventralis; Ctenopoma is neuter, hence breviventrale. The "Grey Ocellatum" differs from C. kingsleyae in that only C. kingsleyae has a conspicuously enlarged silver scale below the eye. It differs from the "real" Ctenopoma ocellatum by the complete absence of vertical bands. Following a study of the type specimen of Anabas breviventralis in the Natural History Museum of Paris, there are currently no serious doubts that the "Grey Ocellatum" from the Congo is the species Ctenopoma breviventrale.
